topics.title: Which modern CSS features do you use for layout and responsive design?
topics.html:
• Container queries — a component reacts to the width of its container, not the window. This is what makes a card reusable in a sidebar and in a full-width page without props like size="small".
  • Subgrid — a nested grid uses the tracks of its parent, so cards in a row can align their titles and buttons even with different text lengths.
  • clamp() / min() / max() — fluid type and spacing without media queries: clamp(min, preferred, max).
  • aspect-ratio — reserve space for images and video, which removes layout shift (CLS).
  • Logical properties — margin-inline, padding-block, inset instead of left/right. RTL support comes for free.
  • gap works in flexbox too, so the old "margin on every child except the last" pattern is gone.
.card-wrap { container-type: inline-size; }

@container (min-width: 420px) {
  .card { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr; }
}

.title { font-size: clamp(1.1rem, 2.5vw, 1.75rem); }   /* fluid, no media query */
.thumb { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; object-fit: cover; }     /* no layout shift */
💬 Say it like this

The one I use most is container queries. Before, a component had to know how wide the page was, so we passed props like size or variant. Now the component reacts to the width of its own container, which makes it truly reusable — the same card works in a sidebar and in a wide page.

Besides that: clamp() for fluid font sizes without media queries, aspect-ratio for images so there is no layout shift, subgrid when cards in a row must align inside, and logical properties so right-to-left languages work without a second stylesheet.

Container queries vs media queries?
Media queries describe the viewport, so they belong to the page layout. Container queries describe the space a component was given, so they belong to the component. In a design system almost everything should be a container query.

topics.title: What changed in selectors and structure?
topics.html:
• :has() — the parent selector everyone asked for. Style an element based on what is inside it: a card that has an image, a label whose input is invalid, a form with an error.
  • Native nesting — write nested rules without Sass. Most of the reason for a preprocessor is gone; variables, nesting and math are native now.
  • :is() and :where() — group selectors. The difference is specificity: :is() takes the highest specificity inside, :where() is always zero, which makes it perfect for library defaults that must be easy to override.
  • @layer — explicit cascade order, so a later layer wins regardless of specificity. It removes most !important from a codebase.
  • Custom properties + @property — typed variables that can be animated, because the browser knows a value is a colour or a length.
.card:has(img) { grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr; }      /* parent selector */
.field:has(input:invalid) .label { color: var(--danger); }

.button {                       /* native nesting */
  background: var(--bg);
  &:hover { background: var(--bg-hover); }
  & .icon { margin-inline-end: 6px; }
}

@property --angle { syntax: "<angle>"; initial-value: 0deg; inherits: false; }
💬 Say it like this

The biggest one is :has(), because for twenty years CSS could not look upwards. Now I can style a card differently when it contains an image, or highlight a field group when the input inside is invalid — things that used to need JavaScript or an extra class from React.

Native nesting removed most of my reasons to use Sass. And I use :where() for base styles in a component library, because it has zero specificity, so the consumer can always override it without a fight.

topics.title: What about UI, motion and performance?
topics.html:
• <dialog> and the popover attribute — native modals and popovers with focus handling, Escape, and the top layer, so no more z-index wars.
  • View Transitions — the browser animates between two states, or between two pages, with a few lines instead of an animation library.
  • Scroll-driven animations — animation progress tied to scroll position, running off the main thread instead of a scroll listener.
  • content-visibility: auto — the browser skips rendering work for off-screen blocks. A cheap win on very long pages.
  • Colour: color-mix() and oklch() — mix and lighten colours in CSS, with perceptually even results. Useful for generating hover and disabled states from one token.
  • text-wrap: balance for headings, and prefers-reduced-motion to switch animations off for users who asked for that.
::view-transition-old(root), ::view-transition-new(root) { animation-duration: .25s; }
document.startViewTransition(() => setPage(next));   /* JS side */

.hover-bg { background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand) 85%, white); }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { * { animation: none !important; transition: none !important; } }
💬 Say it like this

For UI I try to use the native elements first: <dialog> and popover give me focus handling, Escape and the top layer for free, so I do not fight z-index or write a focus trap by hand.

For motion, view transitions let the browser animate between two states, and scroll-driven animations run without a scroll listener on the main thread. And I always add a prefers-reduced-motion rule, because for some users animation is not decoration, it is a problem.
